When we were setting up the catalog for Prettiva & Co., we realized doing this through the standard dashboard UI would take days. Clicking through endless menus for every single size and color variation is a nightmare to debug when you make a typo.

So I built a custom python-based automated parser that takes a structured Excel sheet and loads the variants directly. It was a messy weekend of reading API docs, but it saved us dozens of hours of boring manual work.

Sometimes the best way to speed up your operations is to stop using the shiny web UI and write a script. It is lowkey satisfying to see hundreds of variants upload in seconds.

Our mobile checkout latency on STRAYED was killing our conversion rates.

When we first launched, our Razorpay API redirects took way too long on spotty 4G connections. Users would tap the buy button, stare at a blank screen, and close the tab.

To fix this, we reworked our checkout flow to minimize server-side roundtrips and optimized the mobile redirects. Tbh, a fast mobile experience matters way more than flashy animations.

We managed to shave off valuable seconds from the checkout loop, and the difference in completed orders was instant. People do not want a beautiful loader; they just want their payment to go through.

We built our own custom loyalty rewards engine instead of using heavy third-party plugins.

When setting up STRAYED on MedusaJS, we wanted a unique way to reward our early supporters with custom discounts. Adding heavy external apps felt like a bloat risk for our database performance.

Instead, I wrote the loyalty and referral logic directly into our PostgreSQL backend. It keeps our stack clean, our queries fast, and gives us complete control over how points are calculated.

Hosting it all on our Oracle Cloud VPS means we do not pay monthly SaaS fees for simple features. Sometimes building from scratch is actually the logical choice.

I spent three days making our cart update 200 milliseconds faster.

For STRAYED, we implemented optimistic client-side updates to make the cart feel incredibly fast. When a user clicks add to cart, we update the UI instantly before the PostgreSQL database even confirms the action.

If the server call fails, we gracefully roll it back behind the scenes. This is the exact pattern giants like Amazon use to make shopping feel instant.

People do not notice fast latency, but they definitely feel slow latency. To me, that attention to detail is what separates decent websites from great products.

What techniques do you use to hide latency in your web applications?

Instead, we chose MedusaJS, PostgreSQL, and hosted it on an Oracle Cloud VPS. While Shopify is great for getting started quickly, we wanted complete control over our custom checkout logic and UI.

Plus, hosting it ourselves means we only pay for our VPS infrastructure, which keeps our margins healthy.

Playing Grade 6 Rockschool drums actually made me a better developer.

To drum well, you have to decouple your limbs so they can play different rhythms simultaneously. It is pure coordination, keeping a steady pulse with your left foot while your hands play syncopated beats.

This is lowkey identical to how we handle asynchronous state updates in JavaScript. You have background API calls, UI render loops, and user inputs all happening at different tempos.

Learning to coordinate these independent moving parts without letting the main thread crash is the real challenge.

Earning a black belt is not about executing flashy kicks; it is about doing the basic forms thousands of times until they are second nature. It takes serious discipline and patience.

When our PostgreSQL database migration failed right before a planned update for STRAYED, that same discipline kicked in. Instead of panicking or writing quick hacks, I spent hours reading the logs step by step.

Debugging is just raw patience. You systematically eliminate variables until you find the single misplaced comma in your SQL schema.
